articles.title: Total voters in Mysuru district down to 22.80 lakh from 27.99 prior to SIR
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The total number of voters in Mysuru district has been put at 22.80 lakh with the publication of the final electoral rolls on Tuesday, marking a reduction of about 5.19 lakh compared to the 27.99 lakh voters on the rolls before the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) began on June 20.

The final electoral rolls of all the eleven Assembly constituencies in Mysuru district is available on the official website of the Chief Electoral Officer of Karnataka https://ceo.karnataka.gov.in/ and Mysuru district’s official website https://mysore.nic.in/ , said a statement by the Deputy Commissioner of Mysuru.
The final electoral rolls of Mysuru district comprise 11,15,225 male voters, 11,64,702 female voters and 140 third-gender voters.

While the draft electoral rolls published on August 24, contained 22,42,452 voters, the addition of 44,648 voters and deletion of 7,033 names resulted in the electorate increasing to 22,80,067 as of October 27.
There has been a net addition of 37,615 voters to the draft electoral rolls, according to the statement.

Notices were issued to 1,28,217 voters in the district who were either not mapped or whose records showed discrepancies. Hearings were conducted in all cases, and 1,26,595 cases had been cleared for final publication, the statement added.

The constituency-wise figures released by the Deputy Commissioner show 1.78 lakh voters in Periyapatna, 1.96 lakh in K.R. Nagar, 2.22 lakh in Hunsur, 1.81 lakh in Chamaraja, 2.04 lakh in H.D. Kote, 1.92 lakh in Nanjangud, 2.88 lakh in Chamundeshwari, 1.81 lakh in Krishnaraja, 2.36 lakh in Narasimharaja, 2.14 lakh in Varuna and 1.82 lakh in T. Narsipur.
A total of 31,313 voters aged 18 and 19 years, including 16,584 males and 14,728 females, figure in the final electoral rolls.
The rolls also comprise 30,458 persons with disabilities, 1,112 service electors, 2,750 VIP electors and 179 NRI electors.

Meanwhile, the statement said the process of continuous updation of electoral rolls is under way. Eligible voters can apply for inclusion or deletion of names and for correction of entries in the electoral rolls.

Form 6 is to be submitted for inclusion of a name in the electoral rolls, Form 7 for deletion of a name, and Form 8 for corrections relating to a voter’s name, relative’s name, relationship details, gender, date of birth, address, photograph, change of address, disability status, mobile number linkage and issue of a duplicate Electoral Photo Identity Card (EPIC).

Meanwhile, the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO) of the Mysuru City Corporation held a meeting with leaders and representatives of political parties in Krishnaraja Assembly constituency to share details of the final electoral rolls published after the SIR exercise.

articles.title: Final electoral roll after SSR to be published in Cuddalore on January 4, 2027
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The final electoral roll will be published on January 4, 2027 following the Special Summary Revision (SSR) of electoral rolls, with January 1, 2027 as the qualifying date, Cuddalore Collector and District Election Officer Sibi Adhithya Senthil Kumar said.

Chairing a consultative meeting with representatives of recognised political parties at the Collectorate, he said claims and objections could be submitted from November 12 to December 11. Special camps would be held at polling stations on November 21, 22, 28 and 29 to receive applications.

The revision and rationalisation of polling stations would be completed by November 2. Claims and objections would be received till December 11 and their disposal completed by December 28. The final electoral roll would be published on January 4, 2027.

Applications could be submitted to booth-level officers or at the offices of Electoral Registration Officers and Assistant Electoral Registration Officers. They could also be submitted at the respective polling stations during the special camps. Online applications could be submitted through the Election Commission’s voter portal and the ECINET mobile application.
The Collector has urged eligible citizens to verify their names in the electoral roll and submit applications for inclusion, deletion, correction or change of address within the stipulated period.

articles.title: Keralam Assembly: Govt. has put in place measures to address concerns of expatriates in Saudi, says CM
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Satheesan says the government and NORKA were continuously interacting with various associations of expatriates as well as the Indian embassy and consulate in Saudi Arabia

The State government has put in place a series of measures to address the concerns of expatriate Malayalis in Saudi Arabia amid escalating tensions in West Asia, Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan said in the Keralam Assembly on Tuesday.

Replying to a submission by T.V. Ibrahim, MLA, on the concerning situation in West Asia and the issues of expatriates in Saudi Arabia, the Chief Minister said that any individual cases can be addressed and that the government and NORKA were continuously interacting with various associations of expatriates as well as the Indian embassy and consulate in Saudi Arabia.

He said that complaints received by elected representatives could be forwarded to NORKA for prompt action. A NORKA help desk was opened in Saudi Arabia on October 10 to provide emergency assistance and information to Malayali expatriates and their families. The facility aims to address their concerns, collect details of those requiring urgent assistance and coordinate with the relevant authorities to ensure necessary support.

NORKA Roots has also activated helpline facilities through its Global Contact Centre to provide expatriates with emergency assistance, travel-related information and guidance on the prevailing situation.

The Indian Embassy in Riyadh and the Consulate General of India in Jeddah have established 24-hour control rooms, with their contact numbers made public. Expatriates have been advised to follow the official websites and social media pages of these missions for the latest updates on flight operations, travel disruptions and emergency assistance.

As part of its outreach, NORKA held an online meeting with Malayali expatriates and community organisations in Saudi Arabia on October 24 to assess the situation and identify their concerns. The government is also in touch with expatriate organisations in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries to identify issues requiring urgent intervention and coordinate assistance.

Mr. Satheesan said that the Saudi Arabia government had already announced that visitors holding visit, tourist, Umrah and business visas who were stranded in the country because of flight disruptions could leave without paying fines. He said the intervention of the Keralam government had also contributed to securing this relief.

Arrangements had been made to explore return journeys through airports in neighbouring countries, including Qatar and Bahrain, subject to visa requirements, travel regulations and flight availability. The State government’s representatives in New Delhi were in continuous contact with the Union Ministry of External Affairs, the Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia and the Consulate General in Jeddah to address emerging concerns.

articles.title: Coal India H1 capital expenditure surges 27% to ₹7,966-cr, exceeds target
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: The capex spend in the first half of the fiscal year surpassing the stipulated target of ₹7,286 crore for the period.

State-owned Coal India Ltd (CIL) increased its capital expenditure by 27% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹7,966 crore in the first half of the current financial year, exceeding its stipulated target of ₹7,286 crore for the period.

The miner has utilised more than 48% of its annual capital expenditure outlay of ₹16,500 crore, reflecting a strong investment push towards strengthening mining infrastructure, expanding operational capacity and improving coal evacuation.
Mine infrastructure development, land acquisition, plant and machinery, and diversification together accounted for 79% of the expenditure during the April-September period.

“These strategic investments are expected to strengthen the company’s operational capabilities and support the achievement of its production and supply targets for the ongoing financial year,” Coal India said.

Mine infrastructure development accounted for the largest share of capital expenditure at ₹2,152 crore. The investments were directed primarily towards strengthening coal evacuation and handling infrastructure, including railway sidings and corridors, coal handling plants (CHPs), silos and weighbridges.

Land acquisition was the second-largest expenditure head, accounting for ₹2,033 crore during the first half. The company also spent more than ₹1,000 crore on mine development to facilitate the expansion and operational readiness of mining projects.

The Kolkata-headquartered miner invested ₹1,394 crore in plant and machinery (P&M), including ₹452 crore towards the purchase of heavy earth-moving machinery (HEMM). The remaining expenditure was incurred on washeries and other plant and machinery.

With nearly half of its annual capital expenditure already deployed, Coal India’s investment programme is focused on augmenting mining capacity and addressing potential infrastructure bottlenecks that can constrain production and coal movement. The emphasis on evacuation infrastructure is particularly significant as the company seeks to align its production and supply targets with the capacity to transport coal efficiently.

articles.title: Nayara Energy hikes petrol by ₹5, diesel by ₹3
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: Nayara, which operates 7,108 petrol pumps across the country, raised petrol and diesel prices with effect from early hours of Saturday, October 3, sources said

Nayara Energy, India's largest private fuel retailer, has raised petrol prices by ₹5 per litre and diesel by ₹3 with immediate effect, seeking to narrow the gap between retail prices and rising international oil and refined-product costs, people familiar with the matter said.

The latest increase comes amid renewed pressure on fuel retailers from higher global energy prices and follows a series of price adjustments by Nayara this year as refiners grapple with the impact of geopolitical disruptions on crude and product markets.
Nayara, which operates 7,108 petrol pumps across the country, raised petrol and diesel prices with effect from early hours of Saturday (October 3, 2026), sources said.

Nayara was the first fuel retailer to pass on the surge in international oil prices to consumers when the Iran conflict disrupted energy supplies earlier this year. On March 26, it raised petrol prices by ₹5 a litre and diesel by ₹3, taking the rates at its outlets to ₹100.71 and ₹91.31 a litre, respectively, at the time.
State-owned fuel retailers subsequently began raising pump prices in May.

They increased petrol and diesel prices in a series of staggered moves, with the cumulative increase reaching about ₹7.50 a litre each by late May. The fourth increase on May 25 was ₹2.61 a litre for petrol and ₹2.71 for diesel.

Nayara later reversed its March increase. On July 1, the company cut petrol prices by ₹5 a litre and diesel by ₹3, after international crude prices eased as tensions in West Asia subsided. The reduction was the first by a fuel retailer in more than two years and brought Nayara's pricing broadly back in line with state-owned retailers.
The latest hike, therefore, marks a renewed attempt by the private retailer to pass through higher costs after a period of relatively subdued retail prices.

State-owned oil marketing companies - Indian Oil Corporation, Bharat Petroleum Corporation and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation - control more than 90% of the country's 1,04,137 fuel petrol pumps and have historically kept pump prices relatively stable even when international crude prices fluctuate.
The pricing gap has become increasingly consequential for fuel retailers.
On October 1, the government said private retailers should not cap petrol and diesel sales at their outlets, after Nayara and Jio-bp restricted volumes at some pumps amid losses on retail sales.
Officials said the gap between retail and bulk diesel prices had encouraged industrial consumers to buy cheaper fuel from retail outlets, putting pressure on supplies.

articles.title: Egypt detains prominent journalist Lina Attalah after trial
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Egyptian security forces detained prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah, the chief editor of leading independent news website Mada Masr , after her trial hearing on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), her outlet reported.

A court fined Ms. Attalah three million Egyptian pounds (around $53,400) for operating the website without a licence, the maximum possible penalty for the misdemeanour she was charged with, and ordered Mada's closure.

"Security personnel then surrounded Attalah, lifted her off the ground and took her out of the courtroom, where she remains in custody in the courthouse," said the independent media, which says it has not received a response from authorities about its licence application since 2023.
Her trial marks what rights groups have described as a sharp escalation in Cairo's crackdown on press freedom.
It comes weeks after the high-profile arrest of an entire fact-checking newsroom, on charges of fake news, which are frequently levelled against media seen to be critical of the government.
Hossam Bahgat, head of prominent rights group the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), was present at the court and gave AFP an account of events.

After a brief recess during the hearing Tuesday (October 27), the defence team said the judge ordered the room cleared except for Ms. Attalah and her lawyers, before security officers also entered the room.
Ms. Attalah's eight-person defence team had made procedural requests denied by the court, which then announced it had appointed its own lawyer for the journalist.

"In a move that astonished all those present, the judge recorded in the official court minutes that the court had appointed a lawyer from the Lawyers' Syndicate to represent the defence," Mr. Bahgat said.

"Lina herself spoke up to object to this lawyer being appointed to represent her, which the judge refused to record in the court minutes. In an even more shocking turn, the judge proceeded to dictate motions on behalf of this lawyer -- who had not uttered a single word -- and entered them into the official record," he added.

The judge then announced the three million Egyptian pound fine and ordered Mada's closure "amid shouts and protests from the defence", before Ms. Attalah was detained by the security personnel in the room.
Her defence team is currently trying to secure her release on bail.

articles.title: Syria condemns deadly Jordan strikes as ‘unacceptable violation’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: In the worst crisis between the neighbours since the ouster of longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, Jordan said it had great respect for Syria and expressed regret for civilian casualties
Syria on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) condemned deadly strikes on the country's south a day earlier that Jordan said killed more than 20 jihadists as retaliation for a gun attack on a church.

In the worst crisis between the neighbours since the ouster of longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, Jordan said it had "great respect" for Syria and expressed regret for civilian casualties.

Its Monday (October 26) night strikes came after gunmen last week killed nine people and wounded 25 others during a funeral service at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hammoud in southern Jordan's Karak governorate, an attack that sparked shock across the country.
While Jordan has insisted it coordinated its airstrikes with Syria, Damascus has denied the claim and the two sides have provided differing tolls.
Syria's civil defence agency said the Jordanian strikes killed seven people including three children.

Jordan's government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani said that "the preliminary results... indicate significant losses among Daesh's ranks -- estimated at more than 20 fighters", using an Arabic acronym for the Islamic State jihadist group.
He also said "a large weapons depot belonging to the organisation" had been destroyed.
Mr. Momani expressed regret for any civilian casualties, saying Jordan had avoided targeting locations where it believed civilians were present.
Syria's Foreign Ministry issued a "condemnation and rejection" of the strikes, calling them "an unacceptable violation and breach of Syrian airspace without any prior coordination".
It also said the raid was "a blatant violation of the principles of good-neighbourliness and Syrian national sovereignty".
Amman appeared keen to put an end to the crisis, with Mr. Momani saying that "Jordan holds great respect for the Syrian state and its brotherly people".
Syria said five people including a woman and three children were killed in the village of Al-Taf in Daraa province, which borders Jordan, with two other people killed elsewhere in the south.

articles.title: Lula’s win gives Brazil an opportunity to cement its climate leadership, but challenges remain
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: On a global level, Brazil has come to play a major role in climate negotiations because of its simultaneous status as a major oil producer and, especially under Lula, a strong advocate of international climate cooperation

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva winning his fourth term as Brazil’s President has also interrupted a series of right-wing electoral wins in Latin America. That said, Brazil and Mexico are now the sole left-wing governments among the region’s largest economies. And while it would be reductive to believe the left is more welcoming of climate action and the right is more disdainful, Mr. Lula also faces significant challenges in his role on the issue both in Brazil and beyond.

His foremost opportunity will be to have Brazil cement its mantle of leadership. Brazil is somewhat unique: it is Latin America’s largest economy, the world’s fifth-largest by area, host to most of the Amazon and, crucially, has diplomatic relationships with the European Union, the U.S., China, the BRICS countries, and many other developing economies — potentially allowing Mr. Lula to negotiate across the divides that currently frustrate climate agreements. In fact, China has made tariffs on clean energy technologies a priority for the COP31 summit, set to commence in under a fortnight in Türkiye, with Beijing arguing against protectionist trade measures while the EU and the U.S. have raised concerns about dependence on Chinese manufacturers.

On the regional level, Brazil straddles several problems, including deforestation in the Amazon, illegal mining, forest fires, and a degrading river basin, that demand region-wide cooperation, including the representation of Indigenous groups. Mr. Lula revived such cooperation to a commendable degree through the Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organisation (ACTO), by hosting the Belém summit in 2023, and by making further commitments at the Bogotá summit in 2025.

However, the optimism Mr. Lula warrants is tempered by the Belém Declaration in 2023 failing to establish a binding collective deadline to end deforestation in the Amazon rainforest and to prohibit the development of new oil projects in the region. Both the dependence of the Amazonian countries on agriculture, petroleum, and mining and the powers and resources available to their regulators are markedly different, and political changes are not conducive to sustaining regional cooperation.

Mr. Lula’s fourth term could thus keep ACTO going, especially on cross-border enforcement and in preserving a forum for governments to negotiate on conflicting political priorities. But given the divergent economic incentives and weak national institutions, lasting change means ACTO also developing common monitoring and financing arrangements.

On a more global level, Brazil has come to play a major role in climate negotiations because of its simultaneous status as a major oil producer and, especially under Lula, a strong advocate of international climate cooperation.

In fact, the day after Mr. Lula’s election win, the Netherlands announced that it intends to contribute up to $500 million over a decade, on certain conditions, to Brazil’s ‘Tropical Forest Forever Facility’ (TFFF). The pledge brings the sum of commitments announced thus far to $7.8 billion, against the target of $10 billion by the end of 2026. Lula’s continuing government will help establish the TFFF in its formative years and steady its hand as a potentially new international financial institution.

In the same spirit, Colombia and the Netherlands convened the first international conference dedicated to transitioning away from fossil fuels in April. Fifty-seven countries, including Brazil, participated to develop proposals for financial cooperation, among other matters, and planned for a second meeting in 2027.

As well, at the COP30 climate talks that Brazil presided over last year, Mr. Lula supported proposals to develop an international roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, drawing support from more than 80 countries, but the summit could not see through due to opposition from Russia and Saudi Arabia, among others. The April conference has thus emerged as a parallel mechanism to effect action.

Yet another avenue in the same vein is the EU-Mercosur relationship. The EU and the South American trade bloc signed their interim trade and partnership agreements in January. The latter’s ratification will be significant because they require governments to comply with the Paris Agreement — and could allow Mr. Lula’s climate diplomacy to work through UN negotiations as well as trade and investment relationships to create longer-lasting economic commitments. On the flip side, it may also create greater incentives to convert forestland for other use, so Lula and his peers will have to institute more effective protections.

All this said, while preserving cooperation is essential to effective climate action, it will amount to little if it does not also cut emissions. In fact, continuity in international climate diplomacy could prevent regression without also yielding the acceleration required to meet climate goals. The UN Environment Programme has already found that even if all countries deliver on their pledges vis-à-vis the Paris Agreement, the world is on course to warming by 2.6°C by the end of the century.

Brazil’s incoming conservative Congress is also likely to constrain the Lula government’s ability to sustain expenditure — even if his term provides continuity through 2030, an important year that numerous climate-related commitments use as a deadline or milestone year. That Mr. Lula’s win is a record also raises the prospect of policy whiplash, especially against programmes that depend on his personal political authority, when his last term ends.

articles.title: ‘Cruel’ jail conditions caused dozens of Nigerian miners to suffocate: probe
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Screams for help and banging the door yielded no response from guards on duty, according to survivors

Poor jail conditions led to the deaths of more than 30 miners arrested on suspicion of illegal gold mining in central Nigeria last month, investigators said Tuesday, describing their treatment as "cruel and inhuman".

Thirty-three young men were found dead after they were thrown inside a crowded cell in Minna, the capital of central Niger state, in September after their arrest by the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) , a paramilitary government agency.
Survivors recounted being crammed in the cell with poor ventilation and some said a substance that stung their throats and noses was sprayed into the cell before the door was slammed shut.
Screams for help and banging the door yielded no response from guards on duty, according to survivors.

Medical and forensic evidence showed the deaths resulted from "environmental asphyxia, acute respiratory failure caused by prolonged confinement in a severely overcrowded and poorly ventilated detention cell aggravated by heat stress and dehydration", the head of the investigating team, Jonathan Kure, said while presenting the report to the government.
"The committee concluded that these circumstances amounted to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment," he said.
Niger state authorities initially put the death toll at 37, but the investigating committee said it had established 33 deaths.

"The committee confirmed 33 as the verified casualty figure because higher numbers reported immediately after the incident could not be reconciled with available records and identified victims," said Kure, adding that 14 of the dead were minors.

articles.title: India must make its defence chips end-to-end, say scientists
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: At The Hindu Semiconductor Summit, V.K. Saraswat, A. Sivathanu Pillai and Deleep Nair warn that imported chips leave network-centric weapons vulnerable, and that waiting until 2030-35 for advanced nodes would be too late

India’s increasingly network-centric weapons, from the BrahMos cruise missile to the proposed Sudarshan Chakra air defence shield, will remain vulnerable so long as the semiconductors inside them are imported, senior defence scientists said on Tuesday, calling for chips to be designed, manufactured and packaged end-to-end in the country.

Speaking at the ‘Chips for the Next Battlefield: Semiconductors, AI & the Future of Defense’ panel at SRM Presents The Hindu Semiconductor Summit 2026 here, former Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) Director General V.K. Saraswat said warfare had moved from platform-centric fighting to network-centric operations, in which command, control and communications riding on semiconductors decide the outcome.

“What you saw in Operation Sindoor … is that we are today more or less equipped with complete network-centric capability,” Dr. Saraswat said. Sudarshan Chakra, the multi-layer, multi-domain air defence system announced by the Prime Minister, would fuse data from satellite, sea, air and land-based sensors using artificial intelligence-enabled software, he added. “But we have realised that is not enough for future warfare, for long-duration warfare, to take care of saturation attacks.” Drone swarms, he noted, now arrive “in hundreds and thousands”, and directed energy weapons were needed alongside ballistic missile defence.

A. Sivathanu Pillai, founder, CEO and Managing Director of BrahMos Aerospace, said precision was the point at which chips entered the picture. A BrahMos missile given a target’s coordinates changes course within milliseconds to secure a “bullseye hit”, he said. “How has the intelligence come to that? It is a processor and the software. So semiconductors play a very important role there.” He added that the Light Combat Aircraft Mark 2 could, on a single mission, process as much data as the entire MiG-21 fleet processed in 1971, and that even Chandrayaan-3’s landing was achieved with semiconductor systems that “was all imported, you know; that was our problem”.

Most Indian defence systems are based on 28-nanometre chips, Dr. Pillai said, while the world has moved to 3 nanometres. India is compensating for weaker hardware with software — for instance, by collating data from multiple GPS sources because it does not have a military satellite giving it military-specification accuracy, but that approach would not be enough for hypersonic systems, he argued.

“The government has said that 3 nanometre we will achieve sometime around 2030 to 35. That is too late in the present situation,” Dr. Pillai said, warning that controls on materials, devices and chip-making equipment were coming. “If you want to wait for 2030 to 35 to achieve it, you will miss the bus.” The equipment needed to make a foundry, and not just the foundry itself, would also have to be produced in India, he said.

Dr. Saraswat added that advanced nodes of 5, 3 and 2 nanometres would be essential for AI systems, including large language models and AI at the edge, even if 28-nanometre chips, and perhaps 14-nanometre chips, could carry today’s Sudarshan Chakra requirements.

Deleep Nair, Professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology Madras, traced how far behind domestic fabrication remains. India received complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology from the Radio Corporation of America before Taiwan did, he said, but the Semiconductor Complex Limited (SCL) in Chandigarh was shut for a long period after a fire in the late 1980s. The leading-edge technology running in India today, at SCL, is 180 nanometres, he said, which is the same that Intel, AMD and IBM had in the mid-1990s. Under the DRDO, the Gallium Arsenide Enabling Technology Centre (GAETEC) works on gallium arsenide and gallium nitride, he added.

That dependence carries a security risk, Dr. Saraswat said, recalling how supplies of the 8086/8087 processors used in the first Prithvi missile were curtailed once the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme was announced, and dried up further under the Missile Technology Control Regime. “These devices, if they are compromised while they are being manufactured, then your weapon is compromised,” he said, citing Stuxnet, in which a flaw introduced during fabrication allowed a controller running centrifuges at an Iranian enrichment plant to be remotely overrun. Communication links, foreign cloud infrastructure and foreign GPS-based position, navigation and timing systems posed the same problem, he said: “If the cloud is sitting outside, the entire information going through my network-centric warfare system through the cloud, I am compromised.”

The prescription from the panel was end-to-end domestic capability under the India Semiconductor Mission covering materials, design, manufacturing, equipment and human resources, including compound semiconductors such as gallium nitride and silicon carbide, which sit at the front end of radars and imaging systems. The waiting line for extreme ultraviolet lithography equipment needed for advanced nodes was already four to five years, Dr. Saraswat noted.

Both he and Dr. Pillai called for research and development fabs in the IITs and other universities, on the model of Belgium’s Interuniversity Microelectronics Centre, warning that without them India would again have to import technology for the next generation, such as neuromorphic chips. Dr. Pillai said India already accounted for 20% of the world’s chip design capability. “Why not go in a big way to develop the manpower? Instead of 20%, let us take 50% of the design we should do for the world,” he said, adding that universities should also take up packaging and testing.

Dr. Nair said the Tata fab in Gujarat, being set up with a technology licence from Taiwan’s Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation, would bring the 40-nanometre node, on which a lot of applications could run, while packaging plants were coming up under the mission.

articles.title: Merck drug extends survival in endometrial cancer trial, wins U.S. priority review
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: The drug delivers a cancer-killing payload to cells that carry a protein common in endometrial tumours

The U.S. health regulator has accepted Merck’s experimental targeted drug for a priority review based on data from a late-stage trial where it extended survival in women with an advanced form of endometrial cancer.
The drug, sacituzumab tirumotecan, also known as sac-TMT, delivers a cancer-killing payload to cells that carry a protein called TROP2, which is common in endometrial tumors.

The trial enrolled 776 patients whose cancer had returned or progressed after earlier treatment. Patients were randomly assigned to sac-TMT or to a chemotherapy their doctor chose, either doxorubicin or paclitaxel.
Results showed sac-TMT reduced the risk of death by 32%, with patients living a median of 19 months compared with 12.1 months on standard chemotherapy.
The treatment also reduced the risk of cancer progression or death by 41%, with patients remaining progression-free for a median of 7.2 months compared with 3.9 months on chemotherapy.
In addition, about 35% of sac-TMT patients saw their tumors shrink, compared with 17% on chemotherapy.
A regulatory decision is expected by June 2027, Merck said. The trial data was presented at the ESMO medical congress.

“Based on discussions with the FDA, the company is hopeful for an approval before the PDUFA date to bring sac-TMT to patients as quickly as possible,” said Dean Y. Li, president, Merck Research Laboratories.
Severe treatment-related side effects were more frequent with sac-TMT, affecting about 54% of patients compared with 41% on chemotherapy. About 3% of patients stopped treatment due to side effects.
About 68,000 cases of endometrial cancer are expected to be diagnosed in the United States in 2026, with over 14,000 deaths, according to the American Cancer Society.
Jefferies analysts project peak sales of roughly $900 million in endometrial cancer for the drug and $9 billion across all potential indications.
Merck is developing the drug with Chinese biotech firm Kelun-Biotech, which discovered the therapy.

articles.title: Chip war exposes India’s semiconductor vulnerabilities, industry leaders say
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: U.S.–China tensions underscore need for domestic technology capabilities and resilient supply chains; industry flags gaps in materials, manufacturing expertise and specialised talent

As geopolitical tensions reshape the global semiconductor industry, India needs to develop its own technology capabilities, reduce critical supply-chain dependencies, and build resilience through international partnerships, industry leaders said at a panel discussion on ‘The Chip War: Technology, Geopolitics and India’s Challenges’ at the Semiconductor Summit 2026 in Chennai.

The panellists said India needed to identify areas where it could develop technologies of its own while building domestic manufacturing capabilities and diversifying sources of supply, as countries increasingly seek to secure access to semiconductor technologies, materials and manufacturing capacity.

Sharat Kaul, India representative of the International Electronics Manufacturing Initiative (iNEMI), said the country should not dismiss outsourced semiconductor assembly and testing (OSAT) projects as an inadequate starting point. Semiconductor manufacturing requires specialised equipment, materials, talent and infrastructure, making it necessary to build the ecosystem progressively. “We have to crawl before we walk. We have to walk before we run,” he said.
Mr. Kaul said semiconductor sovereignty did not mean producing everything domestically.

“Sovereignty doesn’t necessarily mean that we do everything ourselves. It means that we build reliance and resilience. A bigger part is really resilience,” he said, citing the importance of maintaining multiple supply-chain options through partnerships with friendly nations.

He also identified advanced packaging, which integrates multiple chips on a single substrate, as an opportunity for India to narrow its technological gap with established semiconductor manufacturing countries.

“The tipping point in the industry is going to be advanced packaging,” he said, pointing to the potential of two-and-a-half-dimensional and three-dimensional technologies amid geopolitical tensions and efforts by countries such as the United States to bring advanced manufacturing within their borders.
Sandeep Garg, chief executive officer and board member of Indichip Semiconductors, said India needed to manufacture semiconductor devices required by its own industries instead of relying on imports.
“The time has come for manufacturing and we have to manufacture our own devices,” he said.

Drawing on his industry experience, Dr. Garg said major semiconductor companies had not established fabrication facilities in India despite being present in the country for decades. India needed to create greater domestic value addition rather than assume its large market alone would attract manufacturing investment, he argued.

Indichip is setting up an integrated device manufacturing facility covering fabrication, assembly and testing, and final modules, with an investment of more than ₹15,000 crore, he said. The company focuses on silicon carbide power devices used in sectors including energy, electric mobility, railways, defence and data centres.
Dr. Garg estimated that India’s silicon carbide market could grow from about ₹13,000 crore in 2030 to ₹1 lakh crore by 2035.

articles.title: ‘India has engineers, but needs more chip-ready ones’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: At The Hindu Semiconductor Summit, industry and government agree the shortage is of industry-ready talent and exposure, and that success should be measured by intellectual property and products, not certificates.

India is not short of engineers, but of engineers who are ready to build chips, panelists said on Tuesday, arguing that the talent gap facing the semiconductor mission is one of practical competence, exposure and experience across the whole value chain, rather than of numbers.

Speaking at the ‘Who Will Build India’s Chips? Bridging the Semiconductor Talent Gap’ panel at SRM Presents The Hindu Semiconductor Summit 2026 here, Ranjith Kumar T.C., Director, PRSsemicon Technologies, said the country had 10,000 to 15,000 engineering colleges and 15 lakh to 20 lakh engineers passing out every year. “The actual shortfall is not the number of graduates that we have. The actual shortfall would be the skilled or the industry ready engineers that we are looking at,” he said, describing the shift needed as one “from knowing to doing,” that is, from learning a concept to bringing out a chip, inculcated during college itself.

Sujhatha, Senior Manager, Guidance, Government of Tamil Nadu, agreed that India was not short of people. India was home to 20% of the world’s semiconductor design talent, she said, but manufacturing was still nascent, leaving a shortfall across outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT), wafer fabrication, materials and machines, which is a gap the India Semiconductor Mission, in its first phase and now its second, has been expanding beyond fabrication and OSAT to address across the ecosystem.

Vikas Makhija, Senior R&D Director, Synopsys Inc., said that the deeper gap was of mindset. Indian semiconductor start-ups had innovated mainly in services, he said, while the United States and China had the real designs. Schemes such as Design Linked Incentive (DLI), which made electronic design automation tools easier to access, and Chips to Startup, under which students could learn the basics and design chips, could change that, he added.

Asked what he wished every graduate entering the industry already understood, Mr. Makhija said industry expectations had never changed. “We still look for the basics,” he said, pointing to core electronics. Tools and languages would keep changing, and artificial intelligence (AI) was now enhancing productivity “by, say, 10x or even 100x”, but only for those who could judge its output. “An average engineer using AI is still not seeing a gain in productivity, but a good engineer using the same AI is seeing 100x,” he said.

Shaik Ayman Hameed Baig, a third-year B.Tech. student in Electronics and Communication Engineering at SRM Institute of Science and Technology and the panel’s student voice, said students tended to become “the first customers for the chip, building projects on it, rather than the true designers”, with many projects in robotics and embedded systems but few in designing chips. With AI automation entering Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) design, students were also confused about what to learn — manufacturing, fabrication or design — he said.

On the mismatch between what companies need and what education produces, the panel pointed to curriculum and exposure. Mr. Makhija recalled that at the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, where he did his master’s in 2006, laboratories were sponsored by companies and students worked on industry projects, and said industry and universities should together design and continuously evolve the syllabus. Mr. Ranjith said the All India Council for Technical Education had restructured the curriculum in 2023 based on industry needs and industry sat on the Boards of Studies of universities such as SRM and Anna University, but the real challenge was dedicated resources and sustained investment, including in centres of excellence. “It is not actually a shortage of talent; it is more a shortage of exposure,” he said.

For Mr. Baig, the most meaningful learning came from a university programme with Sony, working on its Spresense microcontroller with an industry expert. It taught him to submit on a deadline and to take ownership of his work, he said, and, in a conversation with an application engineer who had built the chip, about implementing a programme in Rust, that “there are multiple roles required to get a chip to where it is today and give it purpose”.

Ms. Sujhatha said working life had taught her how painstaking the industry was. “It is all about the yield, end of the day,” she said, pointing to the attention to detail that went into processes starting with a pristine clean room. Mr. Makhija said professional life, unlike college, had no ideal scenario. As a verification engineer whose job was to find bugs, he had learnt to be ready to fail and to find software or hardware workarounds when something was missed. “Things may not be ideal, but you need to figure out a way to make them work,” he said.

A meaningful industry-academia partnership, the panel agreed, should be judged by what students could actually do at the end of it. Beyond just a memorandum of understanding, Mr. Ranjith said, it was about building capability that translated into employment and innovation. “One student whom we train and develop should be developing a chip as well,” he said. Mr. Baig asked for industry to bring real problem statements to faculty and students, and for long-term collaborations. For example, the Sony collaboration, he noted, produced two journal papers. Asked why companies should invest in making graduates employable for other companies, Mr. Makhija likened it to electrons and holes: when one electron left, another came in, and a trained pool benefited the whole ecosystem.

The overlooked roles, the panel suggested, were often the ones that held the chain together. Mr. Makhija traced a chip from product planning and architecture through modelling, design, verification, synthesis and physical design to tape-out, fabrication and lithography, and then post-silicon validation, software bring-up and deployment. “Just think of it like the string of lights that you put up on Diwali. If you just pull out one, it will not glow,” he said. Mr. Baig said design verification, which students assumed was merely checking a design, proved far more complex, since “finding bugs in what is supposedly already right is a really hard job”. Mr. Ranjith pointed to design and register-transfer level work and, in the analogue domain, to analogue design and layout as an even more niche area.

Ms. Sujhatha pointed beyond the chip itself to equipment. Several companies in Tamil Nadu were making semiconductor equipment, she said, and in the current geopolitical scenario, with countries banning imports of certain equipment, even the small components that went into that equipment would become critical in a blockade. The moderator, Nagaraj N, Vice President, Content Analytics and Data, The Hindu , noted that supply chain and logistics roles had proved similarly critical when the industry halted during COVID.

Asked what he wished every graduate entering the industry already understood, Mr. Makhija said industry expectations had never changed. “We still look for the basics,” he said, pointing to core electronics. Tools and languages would keep changing, and artificial intelligence (AI) was now enhancing productivity “by, say, 10x or even 100x”, but only for those who could judge its output. “An average engineer using AI is still not seeing a gain in productivity, but a good engineer using the same AI is seeing 100x,” he said.

Shaik Ayman Hameed Baig, a third-year B.Tech. student in Electronics and Communication Engineering at SRM Institute of Science and Technology and the panel’s student voice, said students tended to become “the first customers for the chip, building projects on it, rather than the true designers”, with many projects in robotics and embedded systems but few in designing chips. With AI automation entering Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) design, students were also confused about what to learn — manufacturing, fabrication or design — he said.

On the mismatch between what companies need and what education produces, the panel pointed to curriculum and exposure. Mr. Makhija recalled that at the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, where he did his master’s in 2006, laboratories were sponsored by companies and students worked on industry projects, and said industry and universities should together design and continuously evolve the syllabus. Mr. Ranjith said the All India Council for Technical Education had restructured the curriculum in 2023 based on industry needs and industry sat on the Boards of Studies of universities such as SRM and Anna University, but the real challenge was dedicated resources and sustained investment, including in centres of excellence. “It is not actually a shortage of talent; it is more a shortage of exposure,” he said.

For Mr. Baig, the most meaningful learning came from a university programme with Sony, working on its Spresense microcontroller with an industry expert. It taught him to submit on a deadline and to take ownership of his work, he said, and, in a conversation with an application engineer who had built the chip, about implementing a programme in Rust, that “there are multiple roles required to get a chip to where it is today and give it purpose”.

Ms. Sujhatha said working life had taught her how painstaking the industry was. “It is all about the yield, end of the day,” she said, pointing to the attention to detail that went into processes starting with a pristine clean room. Mr. Makhija said professional life, unlike college, had no ideal scenario. As a verification engineer whose job was to find bugs, he had learnt to be ready to fail and to find software or hardware workarounds when something was missed. “Things may not be ideal, but you need to figure out a way to make them work,” he said.

A meaningful industry-academia partnership, the panel agreed, should be judged by what students could actually do at the end of it. Beyond just a memorandum of understanding, Mr. Ranjith said, it was about building capability that translated into employment and innovation. “One student whom we train and develop should be developing a chip as well,” he said. Mr. Baig asked for industry to bring real problem statements to faculty and students, and for long-term collaborations. For example, the Sony collaboration, he noted, produced two journal papers. Asked why companies should invest in making graduates employable for other companies, Mr. Makhija likened it to electrons and holes: when one electron left, another came in, and a trained pool benefited the whole ecosystem.

The overlooked roles, the panel suggested, were often the ones that held the chain together. Mr. Makhija traced a chip from product planning and architecture through modelling, design, verification, synthesis and physical design to tape-out, fabrication and lithography, and then post-silicon validation, software bring-up and deployment. “Just think of it like the string of lights that you put up on Diwali. If you just pull out one, it will not glow,” he said. Mr. Baig said design verification, which students assumed was merely checking a design, proved far more complex, since “finding bugs in what is supposedly already right is a really hard job”. Mr. Ranjith pointed to design and register-transfer level work and, in the analogue domain, to analogue design and layout as an even more niche area.

Ms. Sujhatha pointed beyond the chip itself to equipment. Several companies in Tamil Nadu were making semiconductor equipment, she said, and in the current geopolitical scenario, with countries banning imports of certain equipment, even the small components that went into that equipment would become critical in a blockade. The moderator, Nagaraj N, Vice President, Content Analytics and Data, The Hindu , noted that supply chain and logistics roles had proved similarly critical when the industry halted during COVID.

articles.title: Cyclone ‘Arnab’: Flights, trains cancelled as rain batters A.P.; 30,000 boats brought ashore; southern Odisha on edge
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Cyclone Arnab set to make landfall around dawn on Wednesday; A.P. cancels several flights, trains, brings 30,000 fishing boats ashore; Odisha shuts ghat roads, imposes transport curbs, and begins massive evacuation

Heavy rain pounded the northern districts of Andhra Pradesh on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), leaving one dead and a trail of destruction, while southern Odisha remained on edge as the ‘very severe cyclonic storm’ Arnab moved closer to the coast.

According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), the storm is likely to make landfall early — around 2 a.m. to 4 a.m. on Wednesday (October 28) – near the Yanam-Kakinada region in Andhra Pradesh. Initially, the IMD had said that the landfall would take place around forenoon on Wednesday.
Keep track | Cyclone ‘Arnab’ LIVE updates | Storm 140 km from Kakinada; highest danger signal hoisted at Kakinada port

According to real-time information from the Directorate of Economics and Statistics (DES), Jathara premises in Visakhapatnam rural mandal recorded Tuesday’s (October 27) highest rainfall of 141.75 mm between 8.30 a.m. and 7 p.m. Visakhapatnam district, where many places experienced rainfall above 100 mm and strong winds, bore the brunt of the cyclone. At least 200 trees were uprooted within the city limits.

A 65-year-old man died at Mangalapalem after he came into contact with live electrical wires that had snapped and fallen into water. The districts of Vizianagaram, Anakapalli, and Srikakulam also recorded widespread rainfall of above 80 mm until 7 p.m. on Tuesday.

As per the latest information from the IMD, the storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal is moving at a speed higher than expected. As of 5.30 p.m., it was located around 90 km southeast of Kakinada, 170 km south of Visakhapatnam, 170 km east of Machilipatnam, 240 km east-northeast of Bapatla, and 380 km south-southwest of Gopalpur in Odisha.

IMD, Amaravati, Director K. Nagaratnam, who is monitoring the cyclone situation along with her team from Vijayawada, said the rainfall activity, which is centred around northern districts in the morning, would shift to the districts of Kakinada, West and East Godavari, and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema by Tuesday night, when the system moves northwestwards towards Yanam.
ALSO WATCH Watch: Cyclone Arnab: What Andhra Pradesh needs to know

Due to the increasing severity of the storm on Tuesday (October 27), airlines cancelled at least 21 flights in Vijayawada and Visakhapatnam. At the Vijayawada airport, five flights bound for Hyderabad, Chennai, Bengaluru, Visakhapatnam, and Kadapa were cancelled on Tuesday (October 27). The authorities have cancelled all flights on Wednesday as well.

Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu said 290 cyclone shelters had been set up and 84,396 people evacuated to safer locations. More than 30,000 fishing boats had been brought back from the sea, while 93 Andhra Pradesh boats and their crew were reported safe at Gopalpur in Odisha.

The State has mobilised 8,400 personnel to respond to electricity disruptions and is prepared for the possible collapse of up to 15,000 power poles. Teams from the National and State Disaster Response Force, the Navy and the Coast Guard had also been alerted.

Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (APSDMA) Managing Director Prakhar Jain have advised the public to be alert, as extremely heavy rain is expected on Tuesday night in the districts of Kakinada, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema, and Anakapalli. In cases of emergency, one can dial toll-free helplines 1070, 112, or 18004250101.

Traffic on Ennore Expressway and other coastal roads in north Chennai and Tiruvallur district witnessed high waves lashing onto the land as a result of cyclone Arnab on Tuesday evening (October 27, 2026). Residents of Kasikoilkuppam, Ennore, Tiruvottiyur, Bharathi Nagar and Ramakrishna Nagar came out of their homes in panic, seeing the storm surge. Tiruvottiyur MLA N. Senthil Kumar, who visited the spot, said that there was no need for the public to panic. Andhra Pradesh prepares for Cyclone Arnab: evacuations, travel cancellations, shelters activated, with expert insight on landfall and severest impacts.

Cyclone Arnab has uprooted 206 trees across Visakhapatnam, and the Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation (GVMC) had cleared 55 of them by 6 p.m. on Tuesday. Thirty tree-clearing teams are working to reopen blocked roads.

GVMC Commissioner Ketan Garg inspected parts of the East and South zones on his way to Gajuwaka and asked officials to stay in the field and clear fallen trees and debris at once. Sanitation workers have been asked to work through the night.

Only about 2,000 people in Yanam have moved to relief camps so far, with most residents unwilling to leave their homes despite repeated warnings, officials said on Tuesday. The Puducherry enclave, close to where the cyclone is expected to cross the coast, has set up 20 relief camps for nearly 5,000 people.

“Most of them are not willing to move to the relief camps, forcing us to deploy NDRF personnel and local police to persuade them,” Yanam Regional Administrator Shivraj Meena told The Hindu . About 100 NDRF personnel are stationed in Yanam, home to more than 55,600 people, and trees along roads have been trimmed to limit damage.

A 65-year-old man died at Mangalapalem in Visakhapatnam on Tuesday after he allegedly came into contact with live electrical wires that had snapped and fallen into water. A. Pinni Devudu was walking through the water and was apparently unaware of the fallen lines, sources said. The Duvvada police have shifted the body to King George Hospital.

Sixteen flights were cancelled at the Visakhapatnam airport and five at the Vijayawada airport on Tuesday, officials said. The Vijayawada cancellations, four by IndiGo and one by Air India Express, hit services to Chennai, Bengaluru, Visakhapatnam and Kadapa.
Fifteen flights have already been cancelled at Vijayawada for Wednesday, including all 12 IndiGo services, Fly91’s flights and Air India’s morning flight to Delhi, an airport official said.

The Ranchi district administration in Jharkhand has closed schools on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) and Thursday after a rain alert. Eight to nine districts of the State are likely to be affected by the cyclone, Ranchi Meteorological Centre Deputy Director Abhishek Anand said.

The Andaman and Nicobar administration has told fishermen not to venture into the sea till Wednesday (October 28, 2026) and asked operators of tourism and recreational activities on land and at sea to be careful. Rain is expected in all three districts of the islands till October 29, and people in low-lying areas have been asked to stay alert.

Vehicles from Thazhakuppam and Ennore are being diverted via Kathivakkam Bridge and Murugar Kovil road, police said.

In Tiruvallur district, the Collector S. Kavitha has pressed the police, fire services and the revenue department to ensure the safety of the public living along the coast. articles.title: SSB chief to take additional charge of ITBP as D-G retires
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: No regular appointment announced ahead of Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor’s retirement on October 31

The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has assigned the additional charge of Director General of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) to Sanjay Singhal, who heads the Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB), with effect from October 31, when incumbent Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor retires. The ITBP guards India’s 3,488-km border with China.

On October 22, Mr. Kapoor said at an ITBP event in Rajasthan’s Alwar that “face-offs with Chinese troops continue at several locations in Arunachal Pradesh,” leading to a political uproar and demands by the Opposition parties for clarity on the extent of Chinese incursion in the eastern sector.

Mr. Kapoor said, “In the past few days, a situation arose where face-offs happened at several locations in Arunachal, and it still continues. Our Shaurya commandos played an exemplary role in this. ITBP was raised as a mountain guerrilla force, and we were given border guarding duty along China in 2004. We need not leave our original function, and a specialised high-altitude mountain fighting force is being set up, distinct from the Army. We will soon have one full battalion of Shaurya commandos. High-altitude (deployment) is our strength,” Mr. Kapur said.
This was the first official confirmation of the scale of tensions along the northeastern border since July.

On Tuesday (October 27), an MHA order said, “The undersigned is directed to refer to the subject mentioned above and to convey the approval of competent authority for assignment of additional charge of the post of D-G, ITBP to Sanjay Singhal, IPS (UP:1993), D-G, SSB upon superannuation of Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor, IPS (HY:1990) on 31.10.2026 and till the appointment of a regular incumbent or until further orders, whichever is earlier.”

articles.title: U.P. Chief Electoral Officer apologises for ‘tone, language and sharpness’ of social media posts
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: When AAP leader Sanjay Singh questioned CEC Gyanesh Kumar on how ‘Ramhit Yadav’ became ‘Ram ne Yadav ko Maara’ in the U.P. Legislative Council election voter list, the Chief Electoral Officer admitted his responses had not been ‘the kind of communication expected from an official handle’

The office of the Chief Electoral Officer of Uttar Pradesh on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) apologised over the “tone” and tenor of social media posts made by the poll body, following a row over the acerbic nature of the remarks, which pertained to erroneous voter slip entries.

The controversy began when Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) MP Sanjay Singh questioned Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over an erroneous entry, where ‘Ramhit Yadav’ became ‘Ram ne Yadav ko Maara’ (Ram hit Yadav) in the voter list of the recent Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council election.

U.P. Chief Electoral Officer Navdeep Rinwa’s office attributed the error to a translation software glitch. The software used to prepare voter lists was designed to transliterate names entered in English into Hindi, which led to ‘Ramhit Yadav’ being incorrectly entered as ‘Ram Hit Yadav’. The software interpreted the words as a sentence and translated it to “Ram ne Yadav ko Maara” in Hindi.

Mr. Singh had questioned the CEC on whether the latter was running the agenda for a particular political party. “Gyanesh Kumar, why did Ram hit only a Yadav? Why did Ram not hit any Singh, Pathak, Asthana, Sharma, Rai or Bisht? Is your computer casteist? Are you running the agenda of any political party?” the AAP leader said in a post on social media platform X.
In an acerbic response, Mr. Rinwa’s office cited another instance of a similar error, where the name of the father of a voter, Ravi Sharma, was incorrectly recorded as “Ram ne Sharma ko Maara”.

“A bizarre name, ‘Ram ne Sharma ko maara’, has appeared in the voter list for the recent Legislative Council elections. Computers/software are not casteist. We admit that a mistake was made, but fortunately for us, even when the mistake occurred, caste discrimination was not involved,” Mr. Rinwa’s office said.

This was followed by another mocking remark by Mr. Rinwa’s office, which said that had the entry read “Ram hit a minority”, the authorities would have been accused of communalism too. “Thank God, Ram did not kill a member of a minority community. Otherwise, we would have been accused of being communal as well as casteist,” the remark read.

The AAP MP was quick to hit back. On Monday (October 26, 2026), he held a press conference in Lucknow, alleging that the U.P. Chief Electoral Officer was responding like an “agent of the BJP”. He also flagged other absurd entries in the electoral rolls, and sought strict action against Mr. Rinwa for the objectionable remarks.

articles.title: Focus on early intervention at UNICEF workshop on inclusive child development
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Experts suggest intervening when the first signs of autism are identified rather than wait for more to appear

Inclusive early childhood development comprises systems that should reach every child, including those with special needs for whom early interventions can make a significant difference, Vivek Virendra Singh, Lead – Health, Communication Specialist, UNICEF India, has said. He was speaking at a media workshop on ‘Inclusive early childhood development’ organised by UNICEF in association with Press Information Bureau here on Tuesday.

Dr. Singh pointed out that 3% to 10% of the nearly 4 lakh children born in the State could have special needs. He also spoke about district early intervention centres for multi-sectoral interventions for children with special needs.

Deepa Bhaskaran, director, Child Development Centre, Thiruvananthapuram, in a session on ‘Parenting children with spectrum disabilities’ spoke about intervening when the first signs of autism are identified rather than wait for more to appear. Avoiding eye gaze, not responding to being called by name by six to nine months, or not babbling by 12 months were all things that mothers should look out for, she said. She spoke about how to parent children on the spectrum, teaching them emotions, regulating emotions not only of the children but also of parents, coping toolkit, and everyday strategies.

Amar Fettle, State Nodal Officer for Adolescent Health, National Health Mission, spoke on building an inclusive health system, from the primary and family health centre upwards to the CDC, and how these along with systems such as Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) helped in assessment of children and providing appropriate interventions.

Muralikrishna Chinnadurai, trainer, Google News Initiative India Network and AI expert, conducted a session on ‘Using AI for effective storytelling.’ Syam Sudheer Pandi, communications specialist, UNICEF also spoke.

articles.title: Explosions heard over Riyadh as Saudi authorities say Houthi missiles downed
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Houthis accused government forces of killing two people in a strike at a gas station near the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz, where fighting has been intensifying between the two sides

Saudi authorities said they destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen after explosions were heard over the Saudi capital Riyadh on Tuesday (October 27, 2026).
They said air defences destroyed another three Houthi ballistic missiles fired toward the country's eastern region.
Meanwhile, the Houthis accused government forces of killing two people in a strike at a gas station near the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz, where fighting has been intensifying between the two sides.

For weeks, the Houthis have largely encircled Taiz — the capital of Taiz province and Yemen's third-largest city — and cut off most supply routes from government-held areas, but government forces have fought back.

articles.title: Attacks kill at least 60 Orthodox Christians in Ethiopia, church says
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: More than 20 people were seriously wounded, and 20 homes were burned down, the church said, describing the killings as “brutal and merciless massacres”
Two attacks in Ethiopia's Oromia region killed at least 60 Orthodox Christians, the country's Orthodox Church said, urging authorities to protect civilians and bring those responsible to justice.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's Holy Synod said Monday (October 26, 2026) that 14 people were killed in Merti district on Oct. 20 and a further 46 in Shirka district on Oct. 24. Both districts are in Oromia's Arsi Zone.
More than 20 people were seriously wounded, and 20 homes were burned down, the church said, describing the killings as “brutal and merciless massacres.”

Oromia regional government spokesperson Hailu Adugna blamed the Oromo Liberation Army for the attacks. He accused the rebels and their allies of trying to provoke ethnic and religious conflict to divert attention from military losses in northern Ethiopia. He presented no evidence supporting the accusations in the statement.
Adugna expressed sorrow over the deaths and destruction and said regional authorities had begun taking action against those responsible. He pledged assistance to people wounded or displaced.
The OLA could not be reached for comment. Its leader, Jaal Marroo, denied that his fighters target civilians in an interview with The Associated Press published in February.
“Our war is not against the people,” he said at the time.

The OLA is one of seven groups in the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival, formed in September with the aim of removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Other members include the Tigray People's Liberation Front and the Amhara Fano National Movement.
The church said the attacks violated constitutional protections for religious freedom and the right to life. It called on authorities to publicly condemn the killings and prevent further violence.

Oromia, Ethiopia's largest region and home to roughly 40 million people, has endured a conflict between government forces and the OLA since 2018. Other armed groups and criminal gangs also operate there, with civilians facing killings, extortion and kidnapping.

United Nations investigators have accused the OLA of killings, rapes and kidnappings. Human rights monitors have also documented abuses by government forces, including indiscriminate drone strikes, extrajudicial killings and disappearances.

Sarah Kimani, Amnesty International's media manager, told the AP in a January interview that the organisation's research documents summary executions, torture, abductions and rape by both government forces and the OLA.

articles.title: Norway, Finland leaders hold 'frank and substantive' talk with Putin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: "The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," President Alexander Stubb said in a joint statement with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store

Finland's President and Norway's Prime Minister held a "frank and substantive" discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) about efforts to end the war in Ukraine, the Nordic leaders said.
It was the latest effort by Kyiv's allies to de-escalate the most deadly conflict in Europe since World War II, which erupted when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our security and broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," President Alexander Stubb said in a joint statement with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.

Speaking to reporters in Helsinki, Mr. Stubb said the idea for the call had originated during a meeting in Oslo on October 20 between Store, Mr. Stubb and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff.
U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner also took part in the meeting remotely. After the Oslo talks, Witkoff travelled to Saint Petersburg to meet Mr. Putin.

Mr. Stubb said, "Both the Americans and the Ukrainians thought it would be a good idea to reach out," and that Ukraine had wished for the Nordic countries to help it "open a channel of communication".
Store, who was also in Helsinki for a meeting of Nordic leaders, told reporters that the 90-minute call had highlighted "big differences in views" on Ukraine.
According to a statement from the Kremlin, Mr. Putin had during the call stressed that it was the EU's and NATO's "confrontational policy" that was "leading to a protraction of hostilities".
The Kremlin said the three leaders had "agreed to continue maintaining direct contact by telephone".
Mr. Stubb described the discussion between the three as "frank and substantive".
Shortly after the announcement of the call, Kyiv said Mr. Zelensky had spoken to the Nordic leaders about the conversation with Mr. Putin.
The Nordic leaders stressed they were only representing their own countries and had not spoken on behalf of Europe, but Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen bemoaned that they had gone "solo".

articles.title: Record turnout as Israeli voters deliver verdict on Netanyahu
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Israelis are casting their ballots in the shadow of October 7 and the multi-front regional wars that it sparked, with the trauma from the attack still fresh and questions over accountability and security central to the campaign

Israelis flocked to the polls Tuesday (October 27, 2026) in record numbers as a deeply divided electorate delivered a verdict on veteran right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the first election since the October 7, 2023 attack.

After casting his vote in Jerusalem, Mr. Netanyahu expressed worry over high voting among Israel's Arab minority and warned of attempts to "steal the election", a signal of a potential long fight ahead as he echoed his ally U.S. President Donald Trump.

Nationwide turnout as of 2:00 p.m. (1200 GMT) was the highest at that point in the day since such statistics were first recorded in 1973, with the Central Elections Committee giving a figure of 44.9%.

Israelis are casting their ballots in the shadow of October 7 and the multi-front regional wars that it sparked, with the trauma from the attack still fresh and questions over accountability and security central to the campaign.

The close-fought vote comes as Israel looks increasingly isolated on the world stage, driven by the war in Iran and the devastating military campaign in Gaza, soaring settlement construction and violence in the occupied West Bank.

The last opinion polls to be published showed Mr. Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving Prime Minister, running neck and neck with his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, a centrist political novice and former military chief whose mild manner is seen as the antithesis of the incumbent.
Mr. Eisenkot's Yashar party on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) warned that Mr. Netanyahu was "laying the groundwork to challenge the results" of the election.
Before voting, the 66-year-old military man paid his respects privately at the grave of his son Gal, whose death fighting in Gaza has drawn empathy from many Israelis.
Speaking afterwards at a polling station, Mr. Eisenkot called on Israelis to ignore distractions and vote to replace "the worst government since the state was established".

Some 7.3 million people are eligible to vote, with tens of thousands of Israelis estimated to have flown in from abroad for an election seen as crucial to deciding the future character of their country.
Eilana Zisblit, 55, told AFP she had travelled back from Canada, where she had lived for almost 30 years, to vote for a centre-right party in Mr. Eisenkot's bloc.
"The country is going in a really, really bad direction. Both for Jews and Arabs living in the country, and for Jews living abroad," she said.

articles.title: Jaishankar to travel to U.S. for G20 Foreign Ministers’ meet, Quad this week
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Meetings to prepare for Quad leaders’ summit in November, G20 Summit in December; South Africa’s exclusion by U.S. could be raised;

A week after United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to India , External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar will travel to the U.S. city of Atlanta to attend the meeting of G20 Foreign Ministers hosted by Mr. Rubio. The three-day visit from October 29 to 31, which is Mr. Jaishankar’s fourth trip to the U.S. this year, will include meetings with his counterparts from other G20 countries amidst a series of global developments and the ongoing conflict in West Asia.

The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) has not announced the visit thus far, but diplomatic sources confirmed that his engagements will include the Quad Foreign Ministers’ meeting with Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Japanese Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu hosted by Mr. Rubio in Atlanta.

The Quad Ministers earlier met in Delhi in May this year but could not schedule a summit of the leaders in India, whose turn it has been to host the summit since 2024. Instead, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, U.S. President Donald Trump, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will hold a Quad leaders’ meeting in Manila, on the sidelines of the ASEAN-East Asian Summits, that they are all attending in mid-November. In particular, officials are working on ways to take the three key outcomes of the May Quad Foreign Ministers’ meeting forward, including an Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Initiative, the Quad Critical Minerals Framework and the Quad Initiative on Indo-Pacific Energy Security. The decision to hold the Quad leaders’ summit in the Philippines, is a first in a non-Quad country and indicates the difficulties the grouping has had in scheduling the summit in the past few years.

In Atlanta, the controversy over the U.S.’s decision to exclude South Africa from the G20 this year due to bilateral tensions, is also expected to be raised by many of the members. India has thus far not commented on the issue, although others like Russia have criticised the U.S. for the decision, and last week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called for the U.S. to revoke its decision.
When asked, an official said that India has “always supported an inclusive G20”.

All eyes will also be on any possible trilateral meeting between Mr. Rubio and his counterparts from Russia Sergey Lavrov and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi at the G20 Ministers’ meeting. On Monday (October 26), Mr. Trump suggested he was open to holding a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping when he travels to Shenzhen, China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum’s summit between December 18 and 19, after the Manila visit.

Mr. Trump will host the G20 summit from December 14 to 15 at the 800-acre Trump National Doral resort owned by the U.S. President. Mr. Modi will travel to the U.S. as part of a three-stop tour, first to Canada from December 11 to 13, then to the U.S., and after that will fly to Brussels, Belgium to sign the India-EU Free Trade Agreement on December 16.
