articles.title: Nobel laureate Richard Roberts says it’s ‘nonsense’ to fear foreign dependence due to genetically modified crop use
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Dr. Roberts recommends that Indian labs research and own ‘improved agri’ in house; terms Bt cotton a “success” in India; says GM is a question of food and nutritional security for a developing country

Richard J. Roberts, the 1993 Nobel laureate in Physiology or Medicine, on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) dismissed as “nonsense” the idea that Indians adopting genetically modified crops would become dependent on foreign companies. The work can be done in, and owned by, Indian laboratories, he said.

Dr. Roberts was delivering a plenary address at the second Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave (ESTIC), where scientists and technologists from across India gather over three days at Bharat Mandapam. ESTIC is a replacement for the Indian Science Congress, which was last held in 2023 after disagreements between the Department of Science and Technology and the Indian Science Congress Association.

In his address, he rejected the term ‘genetically modified’ as “very misleading” and referred to such crops throughout as “biotechnologically modified,” or BM, arguing that “every life form on this planet has been genetically modified by evolution.”

Asked about fears that an American corporation such as Monsanto (whose operations were subsumed into that of agrochemicals giant Bayer) could control the seed supply and erode the country’s independence, Dr. Roberts replied: “I think it’s nonsense. You can do improved agriculture here in the labs in India and own everything here in India. You don’t have to go to America or Europe or anywhere else to make CRISPR-modified plants. Anybody can do it. You go to a lab, learn how to do it — maybe it takes you six to eight weeks — and then you can do it. It’s really very straightforward because we’ve come a long way in knowing how to improve crops. But you can own it here in India. You don’t have to go to America or Europe or anywhere else.”

CRISPR is a gene-editing tool in which a guide RNA steers the Cas9 enzyme to a chosen spot in an organism’s DNA, where it cuts, letting scientists alter or insert genes at that site. The foundational CRISPR-Cas9 patents, however, are embroiled in an intellectual property dispute.

GM food crops have a contested history in India. In 2010, then-Environment Minister Jairam Ramesh imposed an indefinite moratorium on Bt brinjal, a genetically-modified variant of the vegetable. This was after years of debate on its safety, the financial impact on farmers, and the implications of foreign ownership of the genetic modification technology. In July 2024, the Supreme Court delivered a split verdict on GM mustard’s environmental release, but unanimously asked the Centre to frame a national policy on GM crops. Golden Rice, engineered in 1999 by Ingo Potrykus and Peter Beyer to carry a vitamin A precursor in its grain, has also proved divisive.

Indian researchers reported in the peer-reviewed PLOS One journal in 2017 that backcrossing one Golden Rice transgene event into an Indian variety had yielded stunted, low-yielding plants, unfit for cultivation despite their high provitamin A content.

Asked whether Golden Rice could disturb India’s agricultural systems, citing the invasive spread of eucalyptus. Dr. Roberts said “he was not an expert in agriculture,” underlining that “there are people out there who truly are experts, who I guess can probably answer the questions that you have much better than I can.”

India permits Bt cotton for commercial cultivation, but no GM food crop. Although the Department of Biotechnology promotes GM crops, their commercial release needs the Environment Minister’s approval, and the Minister is not bound by the regulator’s recommendation, as the Bt brinjal moratorium showed.

Kavitha Kuruganti, who leads the Coalition for a GM-Free India, has previously argued that the yield claims for GM mustard, which was cleared by a technical body but whose release subsequently stalled, are not supported by the developers’ own data. India needs a biosafety policy rather than a policy on GM crops, she said.

Dr. Roberts framed GM as a question of food and nutritional security. “Food is medicine,” he said, for people who cannot afford supplements or drugs. Crops eaten in developing countries, he argued, never received the breeding investment Western staples did because their farmers could not pay for it. “Golden Rice is not priced above ordinary rice, and several Indian government institutes hold licences for it,” he claimed.
He added that Bt brinjal lifted yields in Bangladesh and that “no problem” had been seen in 35 years of GM food.

articles.title: Jain seer gives Karnataka govt. 10-day deadline to meet demands; threatens sallekhana in December if demands remain unmet
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Acharya Gunadharanandi Maharaj of Varur Navagraha Teertha Kshetra has given the State government 10 days to provide written assurances on five demands of the Jain community, including the establishment of a Jain Development Corporation.
He warned that he would intensify an agitation in stages and undertake sallekhana (a Jain religious vow involving voluntary fasting unto death) in December if the demands were not met.

Addressing a press conference in Hubballi on Tuesday, he said the government had failed to take decisive action despite repeated representations over the past three years. He said he could no longer remain a silent spectator to what he described as injustice to the Jain community.

The jain monk said the agitation would begin if the government failed to provide a clear written assurance within 10 days. A march and satyagraha would be organised in November, and he would consider undertaking sallekhana in December if the government continued to remain unresponsive.

The five demands include setting up an independent Jain Development Corporation or board; introducing a special security mechanism for the safe movement of Jain monks and nuns; framing regulations to protect Jain pilgrimage centres, temples and historic religious institutions; providing annual free pilgrimage to Shri Sammed Shikharji for economically weaker Jain devotees; and establishing government rest houses or temporary night shelters along the routes used by monks and nuns.

He urged the government to convene a high-level meeting and constitute a joint committee comprising community representatives and officials from the departments concerned. The government should also provide a written response within 10 days, specifying the status of each demand, the department responsible and a timeline for implementation, he said.

If the government failed to respond positively, the first phase of the agitation would involve foot marches to the residences of MLAs in Jamkhandi, Teradal, Kagwad, Athani, Chikkodi, Nipani, Hukkeri and Belagavi to submit memoranda. This would be followed by a large-scale foot march from Chikkodi to Belagavi and a satyagraha, he said.
The agitation would remain entirely non-violent and would not target any political party, he said, appealing to legislators across party lines to support the community’s demands.

The acharya said the demands concerned the development of the Jain community, the safety of monks and nuns, and the protection of its religious heritage. The government should move beyond assurances and provide a written commitment with a clear implementation schedule, he added.

articles.title: A.P. teachers’ body demands implementation of Old Pension Scheme
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The federation leaders allege that the Central and State governments are systematically undermining public education while favouring private institutions

The A.P. United Teachers’ Federation (APUTF) on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) demanded that the Central and State governments protect public education and implement the Old Pension Scheme for government employees.

Speaking at a protest at Dharna Chowk in Vijayawada, as part of a nationwide teachers protest staged under the banner of South Teachers’ Federation of India, the APUTF State president N. Venkateswarlu and general secretary K.S.S. Prasad said that the Central and State governments were systematically undermining public education while favouring private institutions.
They alleged that the government was deliberately weakening the public education system, despite the presence of a large number of students from disadvantaged backgrounds in government schools.

The federation leaders expressed concern over the closure and merger of government schools. Citing a NITI Aayog report, they said approximately 90,000 primary schools had been closed or merged with other schools. articles.title: On the question of KIIFB’s future
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: An expert panel constituted by Keralam’s UDF government to review the functioning of KIIFB has recommended winding it up and absorbing its functions into the State government, prompting a closer look at the merits of off-budget borrowings by States and the need to boost public investment in Keralam

In July, Keralam’s newly elected UDF government set up an expert panel to review the functioning of Kerala Infrastructure Investment Fund Board (KIIFB). The panel, headed by a former civil servant, was tasked with recommending measures to restructure KIIFB and strengthen the government’s institutional capabilities, among other things. The committee has recently submitted its report, which has been tabled in the State Assembly.

Apparently critical of KIIFB’s functioning, the committee has recommended winding it up; absorbing its functions and capabilities into the State government, news reports say. The principal reason for the panel’s recommendation is that with the clubbing of KIIFB’s borrowing function with the State budget, the special purpose vehicle (SPV) has lost its primary purpose.

KIIFB, restructured by the LDF government, reportedly boosted the State’s infrastructure investment by raising extra-budgetary resources, including securing soft loans known as “Masala Bonds” from international agencies after the disastrous floods of 2019. However, the SPV’s functioning and financial performance have remained contentious. The comptroller and auditor general’s (CAG) strictures against KIIFB have become a convenient beating stick for the Centre and the Opposition parties in the State. Leftist critics have branded it as the arm of “the Left Managerial State” for promoting controversial projects, bypassing legislative approvals. In the fog of the debate, KIIFB’s original purpose and economic principles underlying it seem to have been lost sight of. We seek to explain them, intending to shed some light on the contentious issue.

Though Keralam has sound traditional transport infrastructure such as road network and rail connectivity, it lags behind in modern facilities, such as high-speed railways or highways, especially when compared to the neighbouring States. Keralam reportedly spends a mere 1.5 per cent of the Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) on infrastructure. This was so in spite of Keralam’s own-tax revenue to GSDP ratio being among the highest among major States, as per the RBI data.

KIIFB was set up in 1999 and underwent a major restructuring in 2016; the institution’s record in expanding public goods is apparently well acknowledged. However, its functioning raised many queries. The CAG found that the SPV’s finances flouted its procedural audits, which became a sticking point between the Centre and the State. Moreover, as KIIFB functioned outside the purview of the State budget, without generating financial profits from its lending, its borrowings being serviced out of the State’s revenue became the heart of the contention.

In the good/bad old days of “planning”, State finances broadly followed the “gap-filling” approach; meaning the Centre made up the difference between a State’s projected revenue growth and its “developmental needs” as per the State plans. It was a negotiated process, part financial and part political. Evidence shows that richer and politically influential States got the lion’s share of the divisible pool of the plan resources.

The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act (FRBM) 2003 changed that by seemingly imposing a “hard budget constraint”, with the fiscal deficit capped at 3 per cent of GSDP. The RBI now monitors the size of the State debt. The coupon (interest) rate of the State loans depends on the State’s debt sustainability measures. The hard budget constraint has reportedly improved State finances, or at a minimum, made them transparent.

However, most States have devised a variety of means for securing extra-budgetary resources, or off-budget borrowings (OBBs) – as evident from the RBI’s compilation of State finances. The CAG, tracking OBBs, finds that there is a bewildering variety of them. And the actual OBBs are far higher than what it is able to count, as per its own findings. In other words, ensuring fiscal discipline seems like a cat-and-mouse game between the Centre and States. Incidentally, Keralam is not among the worst offenders.

Globally, a variety of financial institutions and fiscal arrangements have existed outside of the budgetary process. Numerous kinds of para-statal organisations are a feature – not a bug – of the fiscal landscape, especially among fast-growing Asian economies. China, for instance, has a bewildering variety of financial arrangements that enable provinces to draw resources from the national development banks to sustain employment at the local level, augment production and exports and ensure political stability. No wonder, China’s public debt to GDP ratio is nearly 300 per cent – though most of it domestic.

Then, realistically, what should be the rules for managing extra-budgetary resources and institutions for Keralam? Simply speaking, if extra-budgetary resources are productively used and they comply with the government expenditure principles, having such off-budget institutions/borrowings may not be undesirable. This follows the Domar rule: so long as the output growth rate exceeds the interest rate on such loans (either at current or at constant prices), they are being used productively. Since such investments have a public good character, individual projects may not be yielding adequate revenue or covering the full costs. However, if in the aggregate they contribute to growth in state output (GSDP) and follow the Domar rule, then such investments are in principle viable.

However, if the State-level SPVs borrow from external sources for social purposes or green financing, which usually have lower interest rates for longer maturities, they need to be assessed differently, as they involve exchange rate risk. Given Keralam’s fragile ecology and need for substantial low-cost resources for protecting it, external borrowing for such purposes by creating SPVs may be desirable, as KIIFB reportedly proved to be after the floods in 2019. The expert committee’s recommendation to dissolve KIIFB is the easier part. In the present political milieu, efforts to boost public investments to catch up with the neighbouring States are a harder job – with the Centre strictly monitoring Keralam. The State will have to devise newer and administratively innovative means to tap OBBs, as most States do. The task is primarily a political one.

dailyQuiz10.explanation:
1. Core Context & Background: Proactive governance kept the casualties low after Cyclone Arnab

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: Cyclone Arnab, the first named storm of the North Indian Ocean cyclone season this year, intensified rapidly before making landfall as a ‘very severe cyclonic storm’ on October 28. This particular rapidity is a challenge for forecasters and some models did fail to anticipate how strong Arnab would become. It also moved faster than expected towards the coast, before stalling for a time and beginning the landfall process several hours before the India Meteorological Department (IMD) had predicted it would, in the middle of the night, leaving many district authorities with a potentially narrower window to evacuate high-risk settlements. With core wind speeds of 125-135 kilometres per hour, it delivered more than 100 mm of rain over parts of Anakapalli, Visakhapatnam, Kalingapatnam, Kakinada and Machilipatnam, in Andhra Pradesh. But even though it has completed landfall, southern Odisha likely faces a greater threat only hence. Early reports claimed no loss of life in Andhra Pradesh or Odisha, which has been attributed to the disaster management operations in both States; the Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister, N. Chandrababu Naidu, said there were five deaths in Andhra Pradesh . Regrettably, the suspension of transport services, including road connectivity and flights, closure of schools and offices, and power cuts to minimise risks posed by loose wires remains an essential part of saving lives, entailing other social and economic disruptions that the States must account for, and address, in their post-storm assessments.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: cyclones / Andhra Pradesh / Coastal Andhra / Odisha / transport / air transport / road transport / economy (general) / Monsoon / agriculture / rains / poverty / disaster management / India / school

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: Benjamin Netanyahu was at the centre of Israel’s October 27 elections. For Israel’s longest-serving Prime Minister, who oversaw a genocidal war in Gaza following Hamas’s October 7 attack , the election was the biggest test of his political career. For the Opposition, which promised to hold him accountable for the failures of October 7 and end the country’s “forever wars”, the election offered an opportunity to oust him from power. The results, however, sent a mixed message. With 85.6% of the votes counted, Mr. Netanyahu’s right-religious coalition has lost its majority but is still the largest bloc . His Likud party is projected to win 26 seats, while its main rival Yashar, led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, is expected to secure 21. Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism, the far-right extremist parties in Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition, demonstrated their continued strength, winning 13 seats between them. The dark horse, however, could be the Arab parties — the Joint List is projected to win 12 seats while the United Arab List (Ra’am) could secure seven seats. With neither bloc commanding a majority, the Arab parties could propel the opposition coalition to power. But the big question is whether the anti-Netanyahu coalition is ready to join hands with the Arab parties, which have historically been kept on the margins of Israel’ s power politics.

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: Operation Trident , a multi-agency crackdown on an international syndicate operating across the India-Myanmar-Bangladesh corridor, marks a significant step-up in the government’s campaign against drug trafficking. The Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has set December 31, 2029, as the deadline to eradicate drug networks across the country. The October 23 raids, which led to 18 people being arrested , were based on NCB investigations following the arrest of an alleged Myanmar-based kingpin in Delhi this May. However, the dismantling of the entire network would require identification of all suppliers in Myanmar and their successful prosecution. The government’s strategy, involving States and Union Territories, over 40 Ministries, central agencies and the pharmaceutical sector, is outlined in the Vision Document on Drug Control (2026-2029), launched by Mr. Shah at the Narco-Coordination Centre meeting on June 26, 2026. It envisages dismantling 100 major cartels and improving prosecution outcomes. The broad strategy reflects the complexity of the problem and signals a more focused approach. Data for 2025 also show an increase of over 50% in arrests and a nearly 53% rise in cases registered under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act compared with 2024.

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The Supreme Court has pulled up, once again, the Rajasthan government over industrial effluents flowing into the Jojari river and the deadly risk it poses for the people depending on it. The problem is decades old — public interest litigation in the Rajasthan High Court alerted State machinery to the problem in 2011 — indicating an oversight by the State bordering on the systematic. The Jojari, the Luni, and the Bandi are seasonal rivers in the State’s arid western region, flowing through Jodhpur, Balotra, and Pali districts. This region has also evolved as a textile-dyeing and steelworking hub, and untreated or insufficiently treated effluents from these factories have run directly into the rivers and soil, endangering the health of around 20 lakh local residents. The region also suffers rampant illegal sand mining in riverbeds. The sewage treatment plants have been able to accommodate only around half of the sewage generated in the three urban centres, according to the State’s submissions to the Court in 2025, even as the Court recorded substantial underutilisation at common effluent treatment plants. The combination is suggestive of industrial sources bypassing treatment facilities, poor connections between the sources and the facilities, and/or insufficient capacity at particular sites or in specific periods.

dailyQuiz10.explanation:
1. Core Context & Background: The National Medical Commission must not be seen as lax on regulation

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has denotified and withdrawn its 2023 Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations (MSMER ), diminishing the framework of penalties vis-à-vis educational standards and infrastructure at medical colleges. The move is noteworthy as the MSMER provided for fines of up to ₹5 lakh on faculty members and administrators for submitting false information. Fortunately, the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) retains the power to fine errant institutions up to ₹1 crore under the 2023 Establishment of Medical Institutions, Assessment and Rating Regulations . MSMER was lauded for its intention to crack down on the deep-seated corruption and malpractice in medical colleges, particularly over ‘ghost faculty’ and ‘ghost patients’. The NMC’s justification is that MSMER also introduced a parallel mechanism allowing undergraduate and postgraduate boards to evaluate institutions, stepping on the MARB’s toes. However, why the NMC scrapped MSMER wholesale is unclear. The 2023 Postgraduate Medical Education Regulations remain in force and include a provision to fine individual faculty members at postgraduate medical colleges. Non-compliance among medical colleges is not uncommon and seldom nipped in the bud, even as the number of medical seats swells while the transparency of the medical education system has not improved.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: medical education / medical colleges / learning / law / corruption & bribery / India / Right to Information

Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: At one point, it seemed almost impossible for Brazil’s 80-year-old President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to turn the tide after finishing second to Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of elections on October 4. In Brazil’s history, no candidate who has finished second in the first round has gone on to win the presidential run-off. Most of the candidates who dropped out after the first round were from the right. Flávio’s Liberal Party cemented its position in both houses of Congress, while right-wing candidates won several provincial elections. But Lula, a former trade unionist and organiser, who lost a finger in an accident as a teenager, was not ready to give up. Lula and his Workers’ Party identified campaign weaknesses, shifted their attention to economic issues, promised growth and welfare, and persuaded more voters to turn out for Sunday’s run-off. Lula won 51.7% of the vote against Flávio’s 48.2%, a greater lead than his victory against Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio’s father, four years ago. Over the weeks, Lula turned the right-wing’s gains in the first round against it, highlighting the threats that a Bolsonaro victory could pose to democracy and civil rights. Flávio’s campaign pledge to free his father — he is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn Lula’s 2022 victory, and impeach Supreme Court judges — only heightened the concerns of voters outside the right wing, who rallied behind a familiar face.
